transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

Based on the symptoms you’ve described (fills, drains, but drum doesn’t turn) and the age of your Indesit/IWC machine (9 years), here is a breakdown to help you decide if it’s worth fixing.

### 1. Most Likely Causes
The fact that it fills and drains suggests the electronic control board, water inlet valve, and drain pump are working correctly. The issue is isolated to the drive system. Common causes include:

• Broken Drive Belt: Very common in older Indesit/IWC models. If the belt has snapped or slipped off, the motor runs but doesn’t turn the drum. Fix cost: Low.
• Failed Motor Carbon Brushes: The carbon brushes inside the motor wear down over time (usually last 5–7 years). At 9 years, they are likely dead. Fix cost: Medium-low.
• Failed Motor Capacitor: If your model uses a capacitor-start motor, this could be faulty. Fix cost: Low.
• Worn Drum Bearings: If the drum feels loose or makes a loud roaring/grinding noise when you spin it by hand, the bearings are shot. Fix cost: High (often not worth it).
• Failed Motor itself: Less common than brushes/belt, but possible.

### 2. Is It Worth Fixing?
Generally, NO. Here’s why:

• Age: A 9-year-old washing machine is well past its average lifespan (7–10 years). Parts are becoming harder to find, and other components (like the tub seal or pump) may fail soon after.
• Cost vs. Value:
• DIY Repair: If it’s just a belt (£8–£15) or carbon brushes (£10–£20), you could fix it yourself for under £30. This is the only scenario where repair makes sense.
• Professional Repair: A call-out + labor + parts will likely cost £100–£200. For that price, you’re putting money into a machine with little remaining life.
• Energy Efficiency: Newer machines are significantly more water and energy-efficient. An older Indesit/IWC model is likely less efficient than a modern A-rated machine.

### 3. Recommendation
Only attempt repair if:
1. You are handy and can follow YouTube tutorials for your specific model (search: "Indesit IWC [your model number] belt replacement" or "carbon brush replacement").
2. The drum spins freely by hand with no grinding noise (rules out bearing failure).

Otherwise, replace the machine.
Given it’s 9 years old, a new machine will likely pay for itself in energy savings and reliability within 3–5 years. Look for a reputable brand with good warranty terms (e.g., Beko, Hoover, Bosch, or Samsung often offer 2-year parts & labor warranties).

### Next Step:
Check your model number (usually on a sticker inside the door rim or on the back) and search YouTube for "Indesit IWC [model] drum not spinning". If it’s a belt or brushes job and you’re confident, DIY is cheap. Otherwise, start shopping for a replacement.

I've looked at the label inside the door and it says IWC 71252. I did notice a faint hot electrical smell a few weeks ago, though not since. Which of those causes should I check first, and how do I do it safely?

The "faint hot electrical smell" is a significant clue. It strongly suggests an electrical component overheated, which points away from simple mechanical issues like a broken belt (which usually doesn’t produce a smell) and toward the motor or its control components.

Here’s how to prioritize your checks, starting with the safest and most likely causes for your Indesit IWC 71252:

### ⚠️ SAFETY FIRST
Before doing anything:
1. Unplug the machine from the wall socket. Do not just turn it off at the switch.
2. Wait 5–10 minutes to let any capacitors discharge.
3. Have a multimeter if possible, but visual inspection is often enough for these common faults.

---

### 🔍 Step-by-Step Diagnostic (Safest to Most Involved)

#### 1. Check the Drive Belt (Easiest & Safest)
While a broken belt doesn’t cause a smell, it’s worth checking first because it’s free and easy. If the belt is intact, move on quickly.
• How: Tilt the machine back carefully (get help if needed). Look behind the bottom panel or through the gap at the front/bottom. You should see a black rubber belt around the motor pulley and the large drum pulley.
• What to look for: Is it snapped, missing, or slipped off? If it’s intact and tight, the problem is likely electrical (motor/brushes/capacitor).

#### 2. Check the Motor Capacitor (Highly Likely Cause of Smell)
The capacitor helps start the motor. When they fail, they often overheat, emit a burnt smell, and stop working entirely. This fits your symptoms perfectly.
• How:
    1. Remove the top panel (usually two screws at the back).
    2. Locate the small, rectangular or cylindrical component attached to the motor with two wires. It’s often black or grey.
    3. Visually inspect it for bulging, leaking fluid, or scorch marks.
• What to look for: If it looks damaged, replace it (cost: ~£5–£10). Part number is usually printed on it (e.g., CBB60 type).

#### 3. Check the Motor Carbon Brushes (Very Common at 9 Years)
Carbon brushes wear down over time. When they’re too short, the motor can’t spin, and the electrical arcing inside can cause a burnt smell. This is the most likely culprit given the age and smell.
• How:
    1. Unplug the machine.
    2. Remove the rear panel (or sometimes front bottom panel) to access the motor. The motor is usually at the back, attached to the drum tub.
    3. Locate the two carbon brushes on either side of the motor’s end caps. They look like small black blocks with springs pushing them against the copper commutator.
    4. Pull them out gently (they slide out).
• What to look for: Are they very short (less than 10–15mm long)? Are they worn unevenly? If so, replace them (cost: ~£8–£15). This is a very common fix for Indesit/IWC machines of this age.

#### 4. Inspect the Motor Wires/Connections
The burnt smell could also come from loose or melted wire connections at the motor terminals.
• How: With the motor accessible, check all wires connected to it. Look for charring, melting, or loose connectors.
• What to look for: If any wires are melted, trim them back and reconnect securely (or replace the motor if damage is severe).

---

### 🛠️ Recommendation: What to Do First?
1. Start with the Carbon Brushes. Given the 9-year age and the burnt smell, this is the highest-probability fix. It’s cheap, easy, and often solves the problem.
2. If brushes are fine, check the Capacitor next. Also likely given the smell.
3. Only if both are good should you consider a failed motor or control board (which would make repair less worthwhile).

### 💡 Final Verdict on "Worth Fixing?"
• If it’s just brushes/capacitor/belt: Yes, fix it yourself for under £20. It’ll likely last another 1–2 years.
• If the motor itself is burnt out or bearings are seized: No, replace the machine. At 9 years old, investing in a new motor (£50+) isn’t cost-effective when a new energy-efficient machine costs ~£300–£400 and comes with a warranty.

Would you like guidance on how to access the motor for your specific IWC 71252 model?

Yes please, I'd like guidance on getting to the motor on the IWC 71252. The machine is in a utility room and I can pull it out from the wall. I'll unplug it first, as you said. How do I get the back panel off, and how do I get the brushes out safely?

Since your Indesit IWC 71252 is a front-loader, the motor is located at the bottom of the machine. You don’t actually need to remove the entire back panel; you just need to access the underside.

Here’s how to get to the motor and replace the carbon brushes safely:

### 🛠️ Tools Needed
• A flathead screwdriver (for clips)
• A Phillips head screwdriver or a Torx T20/T30 bit (most Indesit screws are Torx)
• Pliers (optional, for hose clamps)
• A small container for screws

### 📍 Step 1: Access the Motor
1.  Tilt the Machine: Carefully tilt the machine back onto a soft surface (like a towel or carpet). You may need to lay it on its side if you can’t get enough clearance from behind, but tilting is usually enough for this model.
2.  Remove the Bottom Panel: Look at the bottom of the machine. There are typically two screws holding a plastic cover in place (one near the front, one near the back). Remove these screws and lift off the panel.

### 🔍 Step 2: Locate the Motor
The motor is a cylindrical metal component located towards the front of the underside, just behind where the drum starts. It will have two wires connected to it and a rubber belt wrapped around its pulley.

### ⚡ Step 3: Replace the Carbon Brushes
This is the most likely fix for your "hot smell" issue at 9 years old.

1.  Identify the Brush Holders: Look at the side of the motor (the side facing away from the belt). You’ll see two small plastic or metal caps sticking out. These are the brush holders.
2.  Remove the Brushes:
• Gently pull each brush holder straight out. They usually slide out freely.
• Check the carbon blocks inside. If they are shorter than 1 cm (about half an inch) or look cracked/chipped, they need replacing.
• Also check the copper springs behind them; they should be strong and not broken.
3.  Install New Brushes:
• Insert the new brushes into the holders. Make sure the spring is facing inwards (towards the motor).
• Slide the holders back into the motor until they click or sit flush.

### 🔌 Step 4: Check the Capacitor (While You’re There)
Look for a small black box with two wires attached to the side of the motor. If it’s bulging, cracked, or smells burnt, replace it too. It usually clips on and has two spade connectors you can unplug.

### 🔄 Step 5: Reassemble
1.  Put the bottom panel back on and screw it in.
2.  Carefully lower the machine back to its upright position.
3.  Plug it in and run a short test cycle (like "Rinse & Spin") to see if the drum turns.

### ⚠️ Important Notes
• Belt Check: While you’re under there, double-check that the belt is still on the motor pulley and the large drum pulley. If it’s snapped, replace it (£5–£10).
• Smell Test: After replacing the brushes/capacitor, run a cycle with the door open first to ensure no further burning smells occur.

If you replace the brushes and capacitor and the motor still doesn’t turn (or makes a loud humming noise), the motor itself may be burnt out, which is usually not worth repairing on a 9-year-old machine.

I've had a go and got the brushes out. One is very short with a blackened, charred tip, and the other is noticeably longer. The belt is on both pulleys and feels tight. Is the burnt one enough to explain the drum not turning, and should I replace both brushes?

Yes, that burnt brush is definitely the culprit for the "hot smell" and likely why the motor isn't spinning properly. When a carbon brush gets this short or charred, it can no longer make good electrical contact with the motor's commutator (the rotating part inside). This causes arcing (which creates the smell) and prevents the motor from getting enough power to turn the drum.

### Should you replace both?
Yes. Even though one looks okay, they wear at similar rates. Replacing just the burnt one means the "good" one will likely fail within a few months, leaving you with the same problem again. It’s much better to do it once and be done with it for another 5–7 years.

### How to fit them safely:
1.  Insert into Holder: Slide the new carbon block into the plastic/metal holder so the spring is at the back (inside the motor).
2.  Align Groove: Make sure the copper wire leads are pointing in the right direction for the slot they’ll go into.
3.  Slide In: Push the holder straight back into the motor until it clicks or sits flush. You should feel a slight resistance from the spring pushing against the commutator.
4.  Check Movement: Gently try to wiggle them; they shouldn’t fall out, but they should slide in and out smoothly by hand.

### Final Check Before Reassembly:
• Look inside the motor housing with a torch. You might see some black carbon dust from the old brushes. If there’s a lot of it, gently vacuum or blow it out—just don’t touch any internal wiring.
• Make sure the belt is still tight and correctly seated on both pulleys (motor and drum).

Once you’ve got the new brushes in, put the bottom panel back on, tilt the machine upright, plug it in, and run a quick test cycle. If the drum starts turning now, you’ve saved yourself a lot of money!
